title: Will the Divine app revive six-second loops on social media?
description:
Divine, a short-form video-sharing app, lets users create and share videos which are just six seconds long and repeat on a loop. It’s inspired by Vine, an app founded in 2012 that, at its peak, had more than 200 million monthly active users. It helped launch the careers of some of the internet's biggest stars, including Jake Paul and Lele Pons.

Laura Cress, a BBC tech reporter, explains how the app plans to shake up social media by banning AI and moving away from an algorithm that feeds people videos specific to their taste and browsing habits. Instead it uses an open, decentralized design that encourages people to engage with similar videos as other users.

Plus: Chelsea and Baldeep from the What in the World team re-enact some of the most iconic moments from the Vine era.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討一款靈感源自 Vine 的新短影音應用程式 Divine，該平台主打 6 秒重複循環影片。BBC 科技記者 Laura Cress 指出，Divine 試圖與 TikTok 等平台區隔，除了禁止 AI 生成內容且僅限在 App 內拍攝，更捨棄個人化演算法，採用開放與去中心化的架構，以重現社群共享的網路文化。儘管 Divine 切中了使用者對 AI 內容與演算法的疲倦感，其未來的商業化模式仍面臨挑戰。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores Divine, a new short-form video-sharing app inspired by Vine that features six-second looping clips. BBC technology reporter Laura Cress explains how Divine aims to stand out from platforms like TikTok by banning AI-generated content, forcing videos to be recorded directly within the app, replacing personalized algorithms with a decentralized feed to foster a shared online culture, and navigating the challenge of future monetization without relying on traditional advertising.
